name: Crysthaven
geological_features: Planet-spanning ice sheets averaging 40 km in thickness
Subsurface liquid water ocean heated by hydrothermal vents
Cryovolcanic geysers erupting through fractures in the ice crust
specific_features: The Underblooms — vast forests of photosynthetic flora growing around hydrothermal vents beneath the ice, visible as faint green-blue luminescence through thinner ice regions
Cathedral Fissures — kilometer-wide cracks in the ice sheet where the subsurface ocean's warmth creates steaming grottos
Ice lens formations that focus dim starlight into the upper ocean layers
description: Crysthaven presents itself as a frozen tomb — a world armored in ice sheets tens of kilometers thick, its surface a featureless white expanse broken only by cryovolcanic geysers and the dark lines of cathedral fissures. Surface temperatures plunge well below negative one hundred Celsius, and the thin atmosphere carries only the faintest whisper of nitrogen and trace gases. Nothing about the exterior suggests what lies beneath.

Below the ice, however, Crysthaven harbors one of the most remarkable ecosystems ever cataloged. Hydrothermal vents along a subsurface ocean ridge sustain vast forests of chemosynthetic flora — the Underblooms — that have evolved bioluminescent properties, bathing the dark ocean in shifting curtains of green and blue light. The effect, glimpsed through thinner ice regions, gives the surface an otherworldly glow that early surveyors mistook for mineral phosphorescence.

The Underblooms represent a complete ecosystem built on geothermal chemistry rather than stellar radiation, and their evolutionary complexity suggests they have been developing for hundreds of millions of years in total isolation. The cathedral fissures, where warm ocean water meets the frozen surface, create transitional environments where unique hybrid species bridge the gap between the deep ocean and the ice.

Xenobotanists have identified over sixty distinct flora species in the Underbloom forests, several of which produce compounds with extraordinary medicinal properties including potent anti-inflammatory and regenerative agents. Access remains challenging — submersible expeditions through the cathedral fissures are the only viable route, and the ice sheet's constant movement makes permanent subsurface installations a dangerous proposition.
